title: Routing, ICMP and traceroute
goal: By the end, you can predict which way a router sends a packet, explain how a counter in every packet and a few error reports let traceroute draw a path, say what a line of stars in its output does and doesn't mean, and find out why big packets vanish while small ones arrive.
opening:
Picture the café at closing time. All day its card reader has sent small messages to the payments company's computer in another city, and every one went through. Now the owner taps "download today's sales", a file of a few hundred kilobytes. The app spins, waits, and gives up without an error.

The easy guess is a slow computer at the far end, so you give the app more time. Small messages work, so the road between the machines must be fine. But that road is a chain of machines, each passing messages on without knowing the rest. One of them has a size limit nobody told the café about.

In IP addresses, subnets and NAT, a computer learned to hand anything outside its own network to a router. In this lesson, we'll follow a packet, one small piece of a message, from there. We'll see how each router picks the next step, why a lost packet can't circle forever, how traceroute draws the path, and why the download hangs. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A tool called traceroute lists the machines a message passes on its way, one numbered line per machine. You run it toward a website. Line 4 shows `* * *`, which means no reply came back from the fourth machine, while lines 5 to 9 show machines further along. What does line 4 tell you?
options: The fourth machine throws your messages away, so it's the likely reason the site is slow
The fourth machine passes messages on fine but doesn't reply to traceroute, so the line tells you almost nothing
The path is broken at the fourth machine, and lines 5 to 9 were left over from an earlier run
The fourth machine is busy, so your messages wait there and arrive late
warmup.why: The test messages for lines 5 to 9 had to pass through the fourth machine to get that far, so it passes messages on. Its `* * *` only means that no error report came back from it: it's set up not to send them, or it has sent its quota for the moment. Blaming it is the tempting mistake, because a star looks like a loss. A busy machine would show up differently: as longer times on its own line and on every line after it.

sections.h: How a router picks the next step: the most specific route wins
sections.body:
Let's follow one packet. A packet is a small piece of data with a label at the front that holds two addresses: where it came from and where it's going. The rules for that label are IP, the Internet Protocol, so the label is called the IP header. Each address is an IP address: four numbers such as 10.10.1.10 that name one machine, the way a street address names one house. This four-number kind belongs to IPv4, version 4 of IP. The next lesson meets version 6.

This track's lab network is a few pretend machines on your laptop. Each one is a Docker container: a program that gets its own network card and its own addresses, so it behaves like a separate computer. (A network card is the part of a machine that joins it to one network.) Our packet starts at a machine called client, 10.10.1.10. It's going to ledger, 10.10.4.40, which in our story keeps the café's payment records.

On the way it crosses three links and two routers. A router is a machine joined to more than one network, whose job is to pass packets from one to the next. Client and router share a network called lan. Router and router2 share a link called tunnel. Router2 and ledger share a network called dc, short for data centre, a building full of computers.

Nobody on the way knows the whole path. Each router looks only at the destination address, picks the next machine to hand the packet to, and forgets it. That hand-off is called **forwarding**, and the next machine is the next hop. Think of a chain of parcel sorting offices. A sorter reads the address, drops the parcel in the van for the right direction, and never thinks about it again.

A router makes that choice from its routing table: a list of address blocks, each with a way out. A block is written like `10.10.4.0/24`. An address is 32 bits, or binary digits, 8 for each of its four numbers. The `/24` says that the first 24 bits, here the first three numbers, name the network. So the block holds every address from 10.10.4.0 to 10.10.4.255. That count of fixed bits is the prefix length.

Start with the simplest table that could work: one line that says "send everything to my gateway", the router that leads out. That's the default route, written `0.0.0.0/0`: a block with no fixed bits, so every address fits it. IP addresses, subnets and NAT showed it on client. A machine with one way out needs nothing more.

Router needs more. It has three cards: one on lan, one on wan (a second network, where a machine called server lives) and one on tunnel. A packet for 10.10.2.20 must leave on wan. One for 10.10.4.40 must go into the tunnel, to router2. One for the internet must go to Docker's gateway, the router Docker keeps at the `.1` address of each network.

So a router keeps one line per block it knows about. The kernel, the core of the operating system (Linux, on every lab machine), owns the network cards. It adds a line for each card's own network when the card gets its address. That's a connected route, such as `10.10.2.0/24 dev eth0`, where `eth0` is the card's name. People add static routes by hand: `ip route add 10.10.4.0/24 via 10.10.3.3` means "reach this block through 10.10.3.3". The default route catches everything else.

Now the lines overlap. In the Try it below, you give client one line for all the lab's networks, `10.10.0.0/16 via 10.10.1.2`. Client already has `10.10.1.0/24 dev eth0` and the default. A packet for peer, at 10.10.1.20, fits all three lines. Which one wins?

The rule is **longest prefix match**: of all the lines that fit, the one with the most fixed bits wins, because it knows the destination most precisely. A /24 beats a /16, which beats the /0. So client still reaches peer straight across lan, while packets for ledger go to router. A sorting office works the same way. The pigeonhole for one street beats the one for the whole city, which beats "everything else: send it to the national hub". You can write one broad line plus narrow exceptions, and the order of the lines never matters.

Where do routes come from on the internet? Nobody types them in. Routers tell each other which blocks they can reach, using a routing protocol. Between the networks of different companies it's BGP, which lets an internet provider announce, in effect, "send 104.20.0.0/16 to me". A full BGP table holds around a million IPv4 blocks, and big routers answer the same question for each packet in special chips.

One property matters for everything that follows. Each router decides alone, with no memory of where the packet has been. That lets the internet route around a broken link. It also means two routers whose tables disagree can pass a packet back and forth forever. Next, we'll make two of them do it.

try.title: Add a route and ask the kernel which line wins
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the lab network: `docker compose -f env/net.yml up -d`. Docker Compose starts every machine listed in that file. This lesson uses its second router: `router2` joins router to the dc network through the link called tunnel, and `ledger` (10.10.4.40) sits on dc. The comment at the top of `env/net.yml` draws the whole thing.

Give client one route for every lab network. Then ask client's kernel how it would send to three addresses: `ip route` prints the table, and `ip route get` asks which line a destination would use. Predict each one first: straight across the link, via router (10.10.1.2), or via Docker's gateway (10.10.1.1)?
Last, ask router how it would reach ledger. Router has no route for dc yet. Predict where its default route sends the packet. Leave it that way: the traceroute Try it uses this mistake.
On a Mac, `netstat -rn -f inet` prints your own routing table, and `route -n get 10.10.4.40` asks the same question as `ip route get`.

code.title: in labs/
code.src:
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ip route add 10.10.0.0/16 via 10.10.1.2
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ip route
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ip route get 10.10.1.20
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ip route get 10.10.4.40
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ip route get 1.1.1.1
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router ip route get 10.10.4.40

try.expect:
From one run:

```text
default via 10.10.1.1 dev eth0
10.10.0.0/16 via 10.10.1.2 dev eth0
10.10.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.10.1.10
10.10.2.0/24 via 10.10.1.2 dev eth0
10.10.1.20 dev eth0 src 10.10.1.10 uid 0
    cache
10.10.4.40 via 10.10.1.2 dev eth0 src 10.10.1.10 uid 0
    cache
1.1.1.1 via 10.10.1.1 dev eth0 src 10.10.1.10 uid 0
    cache
10.10.4.40 via 10.10.1.1 dev eth1 src 10.10.1.2 uid 0
    cache
```

The first four lines are client's table. 10.10.1.20 fits /0, /16 and /24, and the /24 wins. That line has no `via`, so client still sends to peer directly. 10.10.4.40 fits /16 and /0, and the /16 wins, so it goes via router. 1.1.1.1 fits only the default. The last answer is router's. It has no line for 10.10.4.0/24, so its default route sends ledger's packets to Docker's gateway, which is wrong. The `eth` number on router may differ on your machine, because Docker numbers a container's cards in no fixed order.

sections.h: A packet that circles forever, and the counter that stops it
sections.body:
Let's break the routing on purpose. Tell router that the block 10.10.9.0/24 is behind router2, and tell router2 that it's behind router. A packet for 10.10.9.9 now bounces between them. Nothing in either table says stop. Every new packet for that block joins the bounce, until the tunnel is full of copies that will never arrive.

That sounds like a lab trick, but real loops happen. When a link breaks, one router hears about it before its neighbor, and for a few seconds the two disagree.

The fix is a counter in the IP header of every packet: the **TTL**, short for time to live. The sender sets it, and Linux starts at 64. Every router lowers it by one before it forwards the packet. A router that receives a packet with TTL 1 may not send it on, because it would arrive with 0, so it drops it. The counter is one byte, which holds at most 255, so a looping packet now dies after at most 255 links. In the Try it below, a ping (a small "are you there?" message) with TTL 64 crossed the tunnel 63 times in well under a millisecond, and then died.

A silent drop would leave the sender guessing. So the router also sends a short report back to the packet's source, like a sorting office that posts a note: "your parcel died here". These reports use **ICMP**, the Internet Control Message Protocol: IP's own messages for errors and tests. They ride inside ordinary IP packets. The IP header has a field that says what's inside. 1 means ICMP, 6 means TCP and 17 means UDP. TCP and UDP are the two ways programs send their data, and later lessons open them up. The report here is ICMP Time Exceeded, type 11.

Every ICMP error quotes the start of the packet that died. RFC 792 asks for its IP header plus at least the next 8 bytes. (An RFC is a numbered document that defines an internet standard, and 792 is the one for ICMP.) Those 8 bytes are enough to hold the port numbers, the numbers that say which program on a machine a packet is for. The sender's kernel uses them to find the program the error belongs to. Linux quotes more, up to 576 bytes in all.

These are the ICMP messages you'll meet. Each has a type and a code, and the code narrows the type down. Ping, the tool, sends an echo request and waits for the echo reply:

| Type, code | Name | Sent when |
|---|---|---|
| 8 and 0 | echo request, echo reply | ping asks, the machine answers |
| 11, 0 | time exceeded | a router dropped a packet whose TTL ran out |
| 3, 0 | net unreachable | a router has no route for the destination |
| 3, 3 | port unreachable | a UDP message arrived for a port no program is using |
| 3, 4 | fragmentation needed | the next link is too small (the last section) |

The router writes its own address as the report's source. A router has one address per card, and Linux picks the card on its route back to you. That's why the Try it shows the error coming from 10.10.3.3, router2's tunnel side.

Two rules stop ICMP from making a bad situation worse. Nobody sends an ICMP error about an ICMP error, or two confused routers could trade errors forever (RFC 1122). And routers rate-limit their errors, which means they send only so many per second. Linux allows a short burst, then about one a second to each destination (`net.ipv4.icmp_ratelimit` is 1000 ms). On top of that, many firewalls, filters that drop some kinds of traffic on purpose, drop ICMP altogether.

**A missing ICMP message is normal. It proves nothing.** Next, we'll turn these reports into a map of the path.

try.title: Build a routing loop and watch the TTL run out
steps: In one terminal, listen on router2 with tcpdump, a tool that prints every packet a network card sees: `docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router2 tcpdump -i any -nn -v icmp`. The word `icmp` keeps only ICMP packets, and `-v` prints each packet's TTL.

In a second terminal, give router and router2 routes for 10.10.9.0/24 that point at each other. Then send one ping with TTL 5 (`-t 5`). Predict first: how many times will router2 see the packet, with which TTLs, and who reports its death?
Send one more ping with the normal TTL of 64, and read who reports it this time. Then stop tcpdump with Ctrl-C, and delete the two bad routes with the last two lines.

code.src:
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router ip route add 10.10.9.0/24 via 10.10.3.3
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router2 ip route add 10.10.9.0/24 via 10.10.3.2
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ping -c 1 -t 5 10.10.9.9
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ping -c 1 10.10.9.9
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router ip route del 10.10.9.0/24
docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router2 ip route del 10.10.9.0/24

try.expect:
The pings, from one run:

```text
PING 10.10.9.9 (10.10.9.9) 56(84) bytes of data.
From 10.10.1.2 icmp_seq=1 Time to live exceeded

PING 10.10.9.9 (10.10.9.9) 56(84) bytes of data.
From 10.10.3.3 icmp_seq=1 Time to live exceeded
```

And router2's capture of the first one (timestamps and the second line of each packet trimmed):

```text
eth1  In  IP (tos 0x0, ttl 4, id 55447, offset 0, flags [DF], proto ICMP (1), length 84)
eth1  Out IP (tos 0x0, ttl 3, id 55447, offset 0, flags [DF], proto ICMP (1), length 84)
eth1  In  IP (tos 0x0, ttl 2, id 55447, offset 0, flags [DF], proto ICMP (1), length 84)
eth1  Out IP (tos 0x0, ttl 1, id 55447, offset 0, flags [DF], proto ICMP (1), length 84)
```

It's the same packet each time (same `id`). It arrives on router2's tunnel card and leaves again twice, one TTL lower each time. Router gets it back with TTL 1 and reports from 10.10.1.2, its address on lan. With TTL 64, the packet crosses the tunnel 63 times and dies at router2, which reports from 10.10.3.3. That whole loop takes well under a millisecond, and tcpdump may miss some copies.

sections.h: Traceroute: draw the path by letting packets die on purpose
sections.body:
Now let's turn the TTL rule into a tool. Send a small test packet, a probe, with TTL 1. The first router drops it and sends back Time Exceeded, from its own address. Send the next probe with TTL 2, and the second router does the same. Keep going until the destination itself answers. That's **traceroute**, which the network researcher Van Jacobson wrote in the late 1980s. It's like posting parcels whose counters say 1, 2 and 3, and collecting the notes that come back.

How does traceroute know it has arrived? Linux traceroute sends each probe as a UDP datagram: a single message sent to a port, the simplest way a program can send data. It aims at a high port that no program uses, 33434 for the first probe and one more for each probe after it. When a probe finally reaches the destination, nothing there is waiting on that port. So the destination's kernel answers ICMP Port Unreachable. Time Exceeded means "one more hop". Port Unreachable means "you are here".

Traceroute matches each answer to its probe by the port in the quoted header. That's one reason the quote must include the ports, and it lets traceroute send many probes at once (16 by default). It sends three probes per hop and prints the round trip time of each. That's the time for the probe to go out and its answer to come back, in milliseconds (ms).

Step through the trace you're about to run. Then we'll read the stars.

A `*` means no answer came back for that probe within traceroute's wait. There are four common reasons. The router filters its ICMP, or it has used up its rate limit for the moment. The probe really was lost. Or the answer had no way back. If later hops answer, the starred router forwarded the probe fine, and the star says nothing about loss. Stars from some hop to the very end are different. Then the path breaks there, or everything from there on filters ICMP, or the destination's answers can't find their way home.

That last case is easy to miss: a reply needs a route too. In the lab network, server has no route back to lan. Its Port Unreachable messages never leave it, and the trace ends in stars, exactly like a dead machine. A TCP connection to it fails the same way. TCP is how programs hold a lasting, reliable conversation, and it opens one with a message called a SYN, which the other side answers with a SYN-ACK. The SYN arrives, and the SYN-ACK goes nowhere.

The path back can also differ from the path there, which is called asymmetric routing. Traceroute shows only the way there, but each round trip time it prints includes the way back.

Two variants help in practice. `traceroute -T -p 443` sends TCP SYNs to port 443, the port for secure web pages, which firewalls that allow web traffic let through. `mtr` repeats a traceroute every second and shows the loss at each hop. Read its middle hops with the rate limit in mind: a router that answers one probe in three still forwards everything.

Traceroute can map a path and show where a route is missing. It can't explain the café's download, where small messages pass and big ones vanish. That needs one more idea: every link has a size limit.

sections.h: Big packets that vanish: link sizes and path MTU discovery
sections.body:
Back to the café's download. Small messages pass and one big file doesn't, so size must matter. It does: every link has a largest packet it can carry, its MTU (maximum transmission unit). On Ethernet, the kind of network most wired machines use, that's 1,500 bytes. In The link layer: Ethernet, MAC addresses and ARP, a machine refused to send 1,473 bytes of ping data over such a link. With 28 bytes of headers, the packet would have been 1,501 bytes. A machine knows the limit of its own link. It has no idea of the limits of links further away.

In the lab network, the tunnel between router and router2 carries at most 1,400 bytes. It stands for a VPN link: a private link between two sites, which wraps every packet in an extra header of its own and so leaves less room inside. Companies join their offices with links like this. Picture a road where one bridge is too low for the biggest vans.

So what should router do with a 1,500-byte packet for ledger? IPv4's first answer was fragmentation. The router cuts the packet into pieces that fit, and the destination glues them back together. It works, and it works badly. Cutting costs the router time, and losing one piece loses the whole packet. Firewalls and NATs can't see the ports in the later pieces, because only the first piece carries them. (A NAT is a router that rewrites addresses, from IP addresses, subnets and NAT.) IPv6 routers never fragment at all, as the next lesson shows.

The answer in use today is **path MTU discovery** (RFC 1191). The path MTU is the largest packet that fits through every link between two machines. The sender sets a flag in the IP header called Don't Fragment, and Linux sets it for TCP and for ping. A router that can't forward such a packet drops it. It sends back ICMP Destination Unreachable, Fragmentation Needed (type 3, code 4), with the next link's MTU written inside. The sender lowers its packet size for that destination and remembers it. Linux keeps the learned value for 10 minutes, and `ip route get` shows it as `mtu 1400`. TCP then sends the lost data again, in smaller pieces.

TCP already agrees on one limit when a connection opens. Each side announces its MSS (maximum segment size): the most data it will take in one packet, worked out from its own card. That covers the links at both ends. Path MTU discovery covers the links in between.

It has one weak point: the ICMP message has to arrive. Many firewalls drop every ICMP packet "for security", a little like a post room that shreds all returned mail to keep the building safe. Then the sender never hears why its packets vanish. The TCP handshake, the few small messages that open a connection, passes. So does a small request. The first full-size packet of the reply vanishes. TCP sends it again at the same size, and it vanishes again. The connection hangs, with no error at all. This is a **PMTU black hole**, and it's the café's stuck download from the opening. You'll make one in the Try it.

The fixes, best first. Never block ICMP type 3 code 4: let it through every firewall on the path, including the ones cloud companies run. On the router at the narrow link, clamp the MSS. The router rewrites the MSS in every SYN that passes, so TCP never builds a packet too big for the tunnel. On Linux that's one firewall rule (`iptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu`). Or let the program's protocol find the size itself by testing with packets of growing size, which needs no ICMP at all.

All three fixes work around the same gap. Routers pass packets along and sometimes report a death, but nothing in IP promises that a packet arrives. Next, we'll see the newer version of IP, and later lessons build the promises on top.

try.title: Make a PMTU black hole, then let ICMP through
steps: This needs the routes from the earlier Try its (client's 10.10.0.0/16 and router's 10.10.4.0/24). It also needs that no big packets went toward ledger yet, because the kernel remembers a learned MTU for 10 minutes. If you've already pinged ledger with big packets, run `docker compose -f env/net.yml restart client ledger` and add client's route again.

Play the firewall. `iptables` is Linux's tool for firewall rules, and the first line adds a rule that makes router2 drop the Fragmentation Needed messages it sends. Then use curl, a tool that fetches a web address, to get a small page and the 300 KB file `settlement.csv` from ledger's web server (a program that hands out pages and files when asked). Predict which one arrives.
Delete the rule (`-D`), fetch the file again, and ask ledger what it learned about the path back to client.

Last, watch path MTU discovery from client's side. Send a 1,500-byte ping with Don't Fragment set (`-M do`, and `-s 1472` bytes of data plus 28 of headers), then a 1,400-byte one, then run `tracepath`, which finds the path MTU hop by hop. Stop the network when you're done: `docker compose -f env/net.yml down`.

```text
From 10.10.1.2 icmp_seq=1 Frag needed and DF set (mtu = 1400)
ping: local error: message too long, mtu=1400

PING 10.10.4.40 (10.10.4.40) 1372(1400) bytes of data.
1380 bytes from 10.10.4.40: icmp_seq=1 ttl=62 time=0.102 ms

 1?: [LOCALHOST]                      pmtu 1500
 1:  10.10.1.2                                             0.047ms
 1:  10.10.1.2                                             0.009ms
 2:  10.10.1.2                                             0.007ms pmtu 1400
 2:  10.10.3.3                                             0.021ms
 3:  10.10.4.40                                            0.025ms reached
     Resume: pmtu 1400 hops 3 back 3
```

With the rule in place, the small page arrives and the big file doesn't. curl got the start of the reply, which says the file is 300,000 bytes, and not one byte of the file itself. Ledger's full-size packets died at router2, and the messages that would have told ledger why were dropped. Without the rule, the file arrives, and ledger now remembers `mtu 1400` for 599 more seconds. The first 1,500-byte ping gets the error from router, and the second fails on client itself, because client has learned the path MTU too. tracepath reports `pmtu 1400` at hop 2, the tunnel.

aside.title: Why do firewalls block ICMP at all?
aside.body: Pings show which addresses have a machine behind them, and floods of pings have been used to swamp machines. So blocking every ICMP message became a common habit. It feels safe, because the only visible losses are ping and traceroute. The real loss is hidden: type 3 and type 11 messages are how machines learn that a packet died, and why, and without type 3 code 4 path MTU discovery breaks the way this section shows. A safer rule lets at least type 3 (all codes) and type 11 through in both directions, with a rate limit if you must.

worked.title: Read an ICMP Time Exceeded by hand

steps.say: This is the answer to traceroute's second probe, captured on client: 102 bytes, printed in hex (base 16, with digits 0 to 9 and a to f), where each pair of digits is one byte. The first 14 bytes are the Ethernet header, the label for the local link. The outer IPv4 header starts at byte 14 with `45`: version 4, and a header of five 4-byte words, 20 bytes. Its protocol byte, at offset 23 (23 bytes from the start), is `01`: ICMP. Its source is router2.
steps.code:
0x0000:  1a77 a5ab e1c1 7a2a 923c d76b 0800 45c0
0x0010:  0058 2cd1 0000 3f01 35f4 0a0a 0303 0a0a
0x0020:  010a 0b00 840c 0000 0000 4500 003c 414f

3f          TTL 63: router2 started at 64, router lowered it on the way back
01          protocol 1: ICMP
0a0a 0303   source 10.10.3.3, router2's tunnel side
0a0a 010a   destination 10.10.1.10, client

steps.say: ICMP starts at 14 + 20 = 34. Its first byte is the type and its second the code. Then come a checksum (a number worked out from the bytes, so the receiver can spot damage) and 4 bytes this type doesn't use. Fragmentation Needed puts the MTU in the last two of them.
steps.code:
0b          type 11: time exceeded
00          code 0: TTL ran out in transit
840c        checksum
0000 0000   unused

steps.say: From byte 42, the message quotes the probe as router2 received it. That's another IPv4 header, 20 bytes again. Its TTL is 1: the probe left client with 2, and router lowered it.
steps.code:
0x0020:  ...                 4500 003c 414f
0x0030:  0000 0111 5f1d 0a0a 010a 0a0a 0428 dfab

45          quoted IPv4 header, 20 bytes
01          TTL 1 when it reached router2
11          protocol 17: UDP
0a0a 010a   source 10.10.1.10
0a0a 0428   destination 10.10.4.40, ledger

steps.say: The quoted UDP header starts at 42 + 20 = 62, with the source port first and the destination port second. `829b` is 33435, the port of the second probe. That number is how traceroute knows this answer belongs to TTL 2, and the lab's `IcmpReport.parse` makes the same walk.
steps.code:
0x0030:  ...                               dfab
0x0040:  829b 0028 197f 4041 ...

dfab        source port 57259 (the kernel's choice)
829b        destination port 33435 = 33434 + (2 - 1): probe 2
0028        UDP length 40: 8 bytes of header, 32 of data

lab.title: A router, a routing table and traceroute
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All 28 fail for now. `Ip.kt`, `Packet.kt` and `Network.kt` are finished: `Network` passes packets between `Node`s, the machines, and makes ordinary machines answer pings and closed UDP ports. The tests build the lab network in `src/test/kotlin/sfz/net/l04/LabNetwork.kt`, with the routes the Try its added.
In `RoutingTable.kt`, write `lookup`: longest prefix match, in two lines.

In `Router.kt`, write `Node.handle`, the decision a router makes for every packet. The comment above it lists the six steps in order: deliver a packet that's for me, drop one that isn't if I'm not a router, check the TTL, find the route, check the MTU, forward. Write a private helper that builds the ICMP error, so the two rules about when not to send one live in one place.
In `Traceroute.kt`, write `traceroute`. It knows nothing about the network: it hands each probe to `send` and gets back whatever answered, the way a real program would.

In `IcmpReport.kt`, write `parse`, the walk from the worked example. The tests feed it four real frames captured in the lab network (a frame is one packet as it crossed the link, Ethernet header included). Run the tests until all 28 pass.
hints: `routes.filter { dst in it.prefix }.maxByOrNull { it.prefix.length }` is all of `lookup`: keep the lines that fit, then take the one with the longest prefix.
Check `owns(packet.dst)` before the TTL: a packet for the router itself is delivered even with TTL 1. Check the TTL before the route lookup, as Linux does.
The error's source is `addressToward(about.src)`, the router's address on the way back. It quotes `about` exactly as it arrived, before any TTL change.
In `traceroute`, accept an answer only if `(answer?.body as? IcmpError)?.original?.body` is a `Udp` whose `dstPort` is this probe's port. Stop when its type is `Icmp.DEST_UNREACHABLE`.

In `parse`, the outer header's length is `(frame[14].toInt() and 0x0f) * 4`. Use `ByteBuffer.wrap(frame).getInt(offset)` for addresses, and `getShort(offset).toInt() and 0xffff` for ports and the MTU.

drill.title: Predict three traceroutes
drill.prompt: No tools. The path is client (10.10.1.10), then router (10.10.1.2 on client's side), then router2 (10.10.3.3 on client's side), then ledger (10.10.4.40). Write the lines traceroute prints in each case, and name the ICMP type and code behind each line that shows an address. (a) Everything works. (b) router2 filters all the ICMP it would send. (c) ledger loses its default route.

answer.src:
(a)  1  10.10.1.2    time exceeded (11/0): TTL 1 died at router
     2  10.10.3.3    time exceeded (11/0): TTL 2 died at router2
     3  10.10.4.40   port unreachable (3/3): the destination answered, stop

(b)  1  10.10.1.2    time exceeded (11/0)
     2  * * *        router2 dropped probe 2 and said nothing
     3  10.10.4.40   port unreachable (3/3): probe 3 got through router2

(c)  1  10.10.1.2    time exceeded (11/0)
     2  10.10.3.3    time exceeded (11/0)
     3  * * *        ledger gets probe 3 but can't route its answer back
     ... * * * until hop 30: it looks exactly like ledger being down

recap: Every router forwards each packet alone: it looks up the destination in its routing table, picks the next hop and forgets the packet. Of all the lines that fit, the one with the longest prefix wins.

The TTL in every IP header starts at 64 on Linux and drops by one at each router. A router that gets a packet with TTL 1 drops it and sends ICMP Time Exceeded (type 11) to the source, from its address on the way back.
Traceroute sends UDP probes to ports 33434 and up with TTL 1, 2, 3, and collects the Time Exceeded reports. The destination's Port Unreachable (type 3, code 3) ends the trace.
`* * *` means no answer came back: ICMP filtered or rate-limited, a real loss, or no route back. Stars in the middle with answers after them say nothing about loss.
Path MTU discovery needs ICMP Fragmentation Needed (type 3, code 4) to reach the sender. Block it and you get a black hole: the handshake works, full-size packets vanish and the connection hangs.

The limit: routers pass packets along and sometimes report a death, but IP never promises delivery and never sends anything again. Traceroute shows only the way there. Programs that need a promise build it on top, as the lessons on UDP and TCP show.
closing:
We started with a café whose small card payments went through all day while one big download hung without a word. Now we know why: a narrow link on the path, and a firewall that threw away the one message that would have explained it.

On a Mac, run `traceroute -n 1.1.1.1` (on Windows, `tracert -d 1.1.1.1`) and count the machines between you and that address. Note which lines are stars, and whether lines further down answer after them. Each star in the middle is a router that forwards fine and stays quiet.

Next, we'll meet IPv6, the newer version of IP, and find out how a machine can give itself an address when nobody hands one out.

quiz.q: A router's table has four lines: `default via A`, `10.0.0.0/8 via B`, `10.20.0.0/16 via C` and `10.20.30.0/24 via D`, where "via B" means "hand the packet to router B". Where does it send a packet for 10.20.31.5?
options: Via D
Via C
Via B
Via A
quiz.why: 10.20.31.5 isn't in 10.20.30.0/24: a /24 compares the first three numbers, and the third one differs. It fits /16, /8 and /0, and the longest of those, 10.20.0.0/16, wins. D is tempting because 30 looks close to 31, but longest prefix match compares bits, not how near the numbers look.

quiz.q: After a link breaks, router X briefly sends 10.30.0.0/16 to router Y, and Y sends it back to X. A machine sends a packet to 10.30.1.1 with TTL 64. What happens?
options: The routers notice the loop on the first bounce and drop the packet
The packet bounces forever, until one of the routers restarts
It bounces until its TTL runs out, and the router that gets it with TTL 1 sends Time Exceeded to the machine that sent it
Y sends the packet back to the machine that sent it, which tries another route
quiz.why: Routers keep no memory of a packet, so neither can see that it has been there before. Only the TTL stops it. Each crossing costs one, and after 63 crossings one router receives it with TTL 1, drops it and reports Time Exceeded to the source. That's the reason TTL exists.

quiz.q: Traceroute to a payments company's web server shows hops 1 to 6, then `* * *` until hop 30. Yet fetching a page from the same server, `curl https://gateway.example/health`, works from the same machine. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The server is down, and curl got an old saved copy of the page
Something near the server drops traceroute's UDP probes or the ICMP answers; try `traceroute -T -p 443`
Hop 7 is losing every packet, so curl only works by luck
The route changes after hop 6, so traceroute loses track of the probes
quiz.why: curl's success proves the path and the server work for TCP on port 443, the port for secure web pages. Firewalls in front of servers often drop UDP sent to unusual ports, or never send ICMP, so the probes die without a word. `-T -p 443` sends the probes as TCP connection requests to port 443, which that firewall lets through. Blaming hop 7 is the tempting mistake: curl's packets cross it every time.

quiz.q: The café's app reaches the payments company through a new VPN link, a private tunnel between two networks. Small requests work, but uploading the day's sales file hangs right after the connection opens. `ping -M do -s 1472`, a 1,500-byte packet that may not be cut up, gets no answer at all, while `ping -M do -s 1300` works. What do you fix?
options: Give the app a longer timeout, so the upload has time to finish
Switch the upload from TCP to UDP
Allow ICMP Fragmentation Needed (type 3, code 4) through the firewalls on the path, or clamp the MSS on the VPN router
Split the sales file into ten smaller files
quiz.why: Small packets pass and full-size ones vanish without an error. So a link on the path is smaller than 1,500 bytes, and the ICMP message that would tell your machine is being dropped: a PMTU black hole. A longer timeout only waits longer for packets that will never arrive. Smaller files don't help either, because TCP still sends each one in full-size packets.

quiz.q: From IP addresses, subnets and NAT: server has no route back to lan, so a traceroute from client ends in stars after hop 1. Now you add that lesson's MASQUERADE rule on router, a NAT rule that rewrites the source of every packet going from lan to wan into router's own wan address, 10.10.2.2. You trace again. What do you see?
options: The same stars: NAT only rewrites TCP connections
Hop 1 is router and hop 2 is server: server answers 10.10.2.2, and router translates the ICMP answer back to client
Hop 2 shows 10.10.2.2 instead of server
Only hop 1, because server never answers UDP
quiz.why: With NAT, the probes reach server from 10.10.2.2, an address on its own network, so its Port Unreachable can go straight back to router. Router keeps a table of the flows it has rewritten (on Linux it's called conntrack). It treats that ICMP error as part of the UDP flow it tracks, and rewrites it back to client. In the lab network the result is `1  10.10.1.2`, `2  10.10.2.20`. NAT handles UDP and its ICMP errors, not only TCP.

flashcards.front: What does a router do with a packet that arrives with TTL 1?
flashcards.back: It drops it, because the packet may not cross another link, and sends ICMP Time Exceeded (type 11) to the packet's source. A packet with TTL 1 addressed to the router itself is still delivered.

flashcards.front: Several lines of a routing table fit a destination. Which one wins?
flashcards.back: The one with the longest prefix: /32 beats /24 beats /16 beats the /0 default. The order of the lines doesn't matter.

flashcards.front: How does traceroute know it reached the destination?
flashcards.back: Its UDP probe arrives at a port no program uses (33434 and up), so the destination answers ICMP Port Unreachable (type 3, code 3).

flashcards.front: What does `* * *` in a traceroute mean?
flashcards.back: No answer came back for those probes: ICMP filtered or rate-limited, a real loss, or no route back. If later hops answer, that router forwards fine.

flashcards.front: What does ICMP type 3 code 4 carry, and what does Linux do with it?
flashcards.back: Fragmentation Needed, with the next link's MTU inside. Linux lowers its packet size toward that destination and remembers it for 10 minutes (`ip route get` shows `mtu`).

flashcards.front: What does a PMTU black hole look like from the outside?
flashcards.back: The connection opens and small requests work, but the first full-size reply or upload hangs with no error. Cause: ICMP type 3 code 4 is dropped somewhere on the path.

flashcards.front: Why does an ICMP error quote the start of the dead packet?
flashcards.back: So the sender can tell which packet and which program it's about: the quoted IP header plus 8 bytes holds the UDP or TCP ports.

terms.plain: A router's list of address blocks, each with the way out for packets headed there.
The machine a router hands a packet to next: another router, or the destination itself.
The rule that picks, of all the routing table lines that fit, the one with the most fixed bits.
Time to live: a counter in every IPv4 header that each router lowers by one. At the end, the packet is dropped.
IP's own messages for error reports and pings, carried inside IP as protocol 1.
The largest packet that fits through every link between two machines.
A path where big packets vanish because the ICMP message that would explain why is blocked.
A router rewriting the MSS in the SYNs that pass through it, so TCP never builds packets too big for a link.

explain_back.prompt: A friend who's learning to program runs traceroute to a website. Lines 5 and 6 show `* * *`, and lines 7 to 11 answer. They want to email the website's owners about lines 5 and 6. Explain to them how traceroute works, and what those lines do and don't tell you.
explain_back.answer: Traceroute sends test packets with a counter, the TTL, set to 1, then 2, then 3, and so on. Each router lowers the counter by one, and the router that gets a packet with TTL 1 drops it and sends back an error report, ICMP Time Exceeded, from its own address. So each line is the router where one test packet died. The website's own machine answers with a different report, Port Unreachable, and that ends the trace. A star only means that no report came back for that packet. Lines 7 to 11 answering proves that the packets for those lines went through the routers at 5 and 6, so those routers pass traffic on fine. They don't send reports to us, because they filter them or limit how many they send. That's no reason to email anyone. If the site is slow, look for the line where the times jump and stay high to the end, or for stars that continue to the very end while the site fails too.

deeper.body:
**Routing inside one company.** Inside a single company's network, routers usually find their routes with OSPF, a routing protocol in which every router tells the others about its links, and each one works out the shortest paths from that shared map. BGP, between companies, is about policy more than distance: which neighbor a network is willing to carry traffic for, and which path it prefers.

**Where traceroute lies.** Big networks spread traffic over several equally good routes (ECMP, equal-cost multipath), usually by mixing each packet's addresses and ports into a number that picks the route. Classic traceroute changes the destination port for every probe, so each probe may take a different branch, and a trace can show hops that are never on one real path. Paris traceroute keeps those fields fixed, so that all probes follow one path; Linux's `traceroute` has `-U` and `-T` modes that fix the port. Tunnels such as MPLS, a way big networks carry packets along fixed paths, can also hide whole stretches of routers, which then never touch the TTL.

**ICMP redirects.** In the first traceroute Try it, router received packets from client and sent them back out of the same card, to Docker's gateway. A Linux router in that position sends client an ICMP Redirect (type 5): "next time, send these straight to 10.10.1.1". Client ignores it, because containers have `net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0`, which is also the safe setting for servers.

**Anycast.** 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8, two free address-lookup services run by Cloudflare and Google, are announced in BGP from hundreds of places at once, and longest prefix match plus BGP's own path choice send you to the nearest one. That's why a traceroute to 1.1.1.1 ends after a handful of hops wherever you are, and why the same address answers from a different city on another network.

**Finding the size without ICMP.** Packetization layer path MTU discovery lets the transport protocol test with growing packets and watch which ones get through, so it never depends on ICMP. RFC 4821 describes it for TCP, where Linux has it as `net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing`, and RFC 8899 does the same for protocols that run on UDP, such as QUIC.

**IPv6.** The IPv6 header calls the TTL the hop limit, and ICMPv6 has its own numbers: Time Exceeded is type 3, and Packet Too Big, the IPv6 version of Fragmentation Needed, is type 2. IPv6 routers never fragment, so blocking Packet Too Big breaks IPv6 even harder than blocking type 3 code 4 breaks IPv4.
